transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood SRE) -- Priya Shah (Novus ML), Tom Rivers (Novus Infra), Alicia Gomez (Novus Product)

Auto-summary (auto/optional):
- Deep dive into observed KV cache evictions and paging on Novus' private deployment.
- Focus areas: prefix reuse, long-context sessions, eviction policy tuning, paging to host RAM/SSD, and how VPC/on-prem latency impacts cache thrash.
- Agreed next steps: reproduce with reproducible load, share trace samples, check infra MTU/packet loss, and iterate config recommendations.

Topics: KV cache architecture, eviction heuristics, paging behavior, prefix-keying, cache warming, long-context perf, batching interactions, quantized model effects, VPC/on-prem network considerations.

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to jump into the KV cache behavior you've been seeing in your private deployment. Priya, can you quickly summarize the problem?

[00:23] Priya (Customer): Yeah, thanks. So we've been noticing a lot of higher tail latency spikes and token-generation slowdowns for some long-session users. It looks like the cache is evicting more than we expect when sessions have a reused prefix (e.g., long system prompt + repeated user prompts). We see those evictions followed by paging events and occasional OOM warnings at the node level.

[00:45] Liam (SE): Quick question, Priya — when you say "reused prefix", is this single session reusing the same prefix across multiple requests or are multiple sessions sharing the same prefix text?

[00:54] Priya: It's both. We have a canonical medical history prompt that's attached to many sessions and users append short real-time conversation after that. So prefix reuse across sessions is common. Also some sessions are super long: 30k+ tokens in the KV.

[01:12] Tom (Infra): To add, we're on-prem with a VPC-esque overlay and we use Redwood Private. We saw that eviction metrics spike during higher concurrency periods. We also saw host paging to disk at times when several long sessions were active.

[01:32] Carlos (Redwood SRE): Thanks. A couple of framing pieces from the runtime: Redwood's KV cache keys are session-scoped hashes plus prefix-id metadata. By default we do LRU-ish eviction with soft thresholds to avoid immediate OOMs; however, if memory is exhausted we page to host RAM and then to swap/SSD depending on your deployment config. Paging in on-prem setups can be quite expensive.

[01:52] Alicia (Product): Do you have guidance on prefix-hashing or grouping? Could we be colliding keys or duplicating stored KV frames?

[02:05] Liam: Great question. We don't usually see collisions at a hash-level; more often what's observed is duplicate storage because clients open new session IDs for logically related conversations instead of reusing the same session ID. That leads to multiple KV entries with largely overlapping content. If your client creates 1k ephemeral sessions that share a 15k-token prefix, that's 1k * 15k tokens of KV stored.

[02:29] Priya: Huh okay. We do create new session ids for each visit for auditing reasons. We thought that would reduce cross-session leakage, but it bloats the cache.

[02:40] Maya: Two separate levers: client-side session management (prefer prefix reuse on same session ID when safe), and server-side dedupe/warm-on-write. We can show you config options for prefix canonicalization so identical prefix content maps to shared prefix entries rather than duplicated KV per session id.

[03:02] Tom: Walk me through paging tiers — when does Redwood runtime page from GPU to host and then to disk?

[03:12] Carlos: Simplified sequence: active KV shard memory is first on GPU device memory; when that exceeds the soft threshold we move less-recent entries to pinned host RAM (fast path), and only when host RAM is under pressure do we swap to SSD or swapfile depending on your node. On-prem with high I/O latency or small SSDs will see much worse performance once we hit that last tier.

[03:36] Priya: The slowdowns correlate with increased swap usage on the node, yeah.

[03:41] Liam: Two important troubleshooting steps we recommend: 1) capture a flamegraph + KV hit/miss timeline from the Redwood instrumentation (we'll send the exact queries), and 2) run a synthetic workload that reproduces your prefix reuse shape so we can isolate whether the problem is pure memory pressure or also a pathological access pattern that causes churn.

[03:59] Priya: We'll share traces. Also, we suspect that quantized model runtimes have a different KV memory shape — like the cache items are smaller but more numerous. Anything to watch there?

[04:12] Liam: Yes — quantization changes internal tensor layout and sometimes alignment, which affects how we pack KV frames. You might see different eviction thresholds and fragmentation patterns. For example 4-bit quant runs may store keys differently; fragmentation causes more frequent paging even if nominal memory usage looks similar. We can surface per-model KV footprint in the console.

[04:35] Alicia: Is there any batching interaction? We noticed that enabling aggressive batching seemed to increase effective memory, or at least the spikes.

[04:44] Carlos: Batching doesn't directly increase KV size, but it increases concurrent active contexts and the number of in-flight KV lookups; that can raise peak memory temporally and make the soft eviction thresholds trigger more often. Also continuous batching widens the window of concurrency.

[05:02] Tom: On our infra side, sometimes we see packet drops and retransmits between nodes in the overlay. Could network jitter cause apparent evictions?

[05:12] Maya: Yes — if the runtime waits on KV shard responses from a remote node or if there's retransmit, it can artificially increase latency and, if requests get queued, memory pressure can build and cause eviction. On VPC/on-prem with additional egress hops, tune the replica placement and increase the soft memory headroom.

[05:33] Priya: We're also doing a lot of prefix reuse where an identical 10k-token medical summary is attached to thousands of sessions. Is the right pattern to canonicalize that prefix server-side?

[05:45] Liam: For high reuse content, canonicalization + shared prefix entries is ideal. Two approaches: 1) client-provided prefix-id: your client computes a stable digest and sends that with requests (runtime treats digest as a shared prefix entry), or 2) server-side dedupe: Redwood can enable optional prefix canonicalization in the private control plane so identical prefix blobs map to a single stored KV record and are referenced by multiple session ids. Both have tradeoffs around auditability and session isolation.

[06:13] Priya: For audit reasons we do need to track which user saw what, but maybe we can store prefix once and keep per-session small metadata pointers.

[06:21] Maya: Exactly. You can keep per-session metadata and pointer references to the canonical prefix; that reduces memory while keeping traceability. We'll share a recommended pattern doc.

[06:32] Tom: What about eviction policy tuning — can we change from LRU to TTL or weighted policy? We have some prefixes that are truly hot and others that are cold.

[06:44] Carlos: You can configure per-workload policies: TTL-based eviction for ephemeral prefixes, weighted LRU for prioritizing smaller entries or entries with higher hit rates, and pinning for critical prefixes. Pinning keeps KV entries resident in GPU memory across restarts, but obviously increases memory consumption. We recommend a mixed policy: pin a small set of known-hot prefixes, TTL for audit logs that are short-lived, and LRU for everything else.

[07:12] Priya: How do we detect collisions or accidental key duplication? Any metric for duplicate content stored across session ids?

[07:22] Liam: We'll provide a dedupe report query. Typically you look at a "prefix-fingerprint -> distinct-session-count" metric; a high distinct count with identical size and hash suggests duplicated storage. We also provide a KV inefficiency radar in Redwood Console (we'll share link).

[07:41] Alicia: You mentioned soft thresholds — can you explain how they behave under bursts?

[07:48] Carlos: Soft thresholds attempt to preemptively move entries off GPU to host before an OOM, using heuristics over recent access patterns. Under a short burst you'll see a transient move and then possibly a warm-up as requests bring items back in. If bursts are frequent, churn will increase and that manifests as high eviction and refill rates. You can increase soft threshold headroom or tune the backpressure policy to reject non-critical requests during pressure spikes.

[08:17] Priya: We also saw evidence that some prefixes were being evicted while still hot — maybe because their size is large and eviction picks by token size rather than recency?

[08:27] Liam: The default policy considers both recency and size (we use a cost metric). Very large prefix frames can be evicted to free space even if they've been used recently, because their cost-to-keep is high. You can set weights to prefer keeping recent small entries over large ones, or split large prefixes into smaller chunked frames so eviction can be more granular.

[08:52] Tom: Chunking sounds promising. Does chunking affect prefix reuse/dedupe?

[08:58] Liam: It does. If you canonicalize and then chunk, you can share chunks across sessions; dedupe operates at the chunk-fingerprint level. Chunk size is configurable; too small increases metadata overhead, too large reduces eviction granularity. We'll provide a recommended chunk-size for common long-context LLMs.

[09:19] Priya: Any gotchas with on-prem KMS and KV stored in host RAM or disk? We encrypt at rest but not all nodes have HSMs.

[09:28] Carlos: KV frames in host RAM will be encrypted at rest if written to disk, but in-memory pages are plaintext by necessity. If you require in-use encryption, we have integrations with HSM/KMS and confidential compute in some deployments — but that has performance tradeoffs. We can model the perf hit for your expected workload.

[09:47] Alicia: Could quantization cause key mismatch across model variants causing duplicated KV per-variant?

[09:53] Liam: Yes. If you route to multiple model variants (e.g., quantized v1 vs float16 v2) and the key derivation depends on internal model tokenization differences, the same logical prefix could map to different KV fingerprints. To avoid that, ensure tokenization is deterministic across variants or canonicalize at application layer before sending.

[10:12] Priya: We did have a canary that used a different tokenizer and saw duplicated storage. Good catch.

[10:18] Maya: Practical triage checklist we propose:
- Collect a 10-minute sample window from your busiest period (KV hit/miss, eviction rates, swap usage, in-flight batch count).
- Run Redwood's prefix-dedupe report and chunking suggestions.
- Reproduce with synthetic runner that mirrors your session creation patterns (we'll provide runner).
- If paging persists, increase soft threshold or add pinned instances for hot prefixes.

[10:49] Priya: For the synthetic runner, can you simulate our audit constraints (session-per-user creation)?

[10:54] Liam: Yes, we can parameterize two modes: session-per-user and shared-session-with-metadata. We'll simulate both to show memory delta.

[11:03] Carlos: Also, check your node-level cgroups and kube eviction thresholds if you run on K8s. We had a customer where kube_protect caused host OOMkill because kubelet's eviction was more aggressive than runtime's soft-eviction.

[11:21] Tom: We're on VMs. How do we see if network jitter is causing request queuing?

[11:27] Maya: Look at request queuing metrics in Redwood Console (per-shard request latency P50/P95), and correlate with kernel retransmit counters on your infra. We'll send the exact Grafana queries.

[11:38] Priya: Any immediate low-effort knobs we can flip?

[11:41] Liam: Yes: enable prefix canonicalization for the largest shared prompts, raise soft threshold headroom by 10-20% temporarily, and pin top 20 hot prefixes. Also disable cross-variant routing until tokenization is aligned.

[11:56] Alicia: What's the expected perf delta for pinning 20 prefixes?

[12:01] Carlos: Depends on size. If they're small (<=4k tokens), you should see reduced P95 tail latency by ~15-30% under load. If large, benefit is lower per memory cost. We'll estimate after we see your actual prefix sizes.

[12:19] Priya: We'll extract three example prefixes and send them to you. We will anonymize them first.

[12:25] Maya: Great. After that, we'll run a synthesis: Liam will produce reproducer traces, Carlos will look at host metrics, Priya and Tom will share the sample prefixes and infra details. We'll regroup after the reproducer.

[12:40] Tom: One more question — any implications for billing or Dedicated capacity sizing? If we pin a lot will we need larger Dedicated commitment?

[12:49] Maya: Yes, pinning and larger headroom will increase memory footprint and potentially push you to a larger GPU SKU or more nodes. There's a tradeoff: paying for more reserved capacity vs higher latency/cost-per-token from frequent paging. Redwood Optimize can run a sizing analysis for your workload; we can share that estimate.

[13:10] Priya: Ok cool. Anything else?

[13:14] Liam: I'll also check for any subtle bug we recently fixed around chunk boundary handling that could cause duplicate keys when chunking large prefixes — not likely but worth ruling out.

[13:24] Maya: Recap of immediate next steps: 1) Novus provides anonymized prefix samples and session pattern summary; 2) Redwood runs reproducer and shares KV instrumentation dashboard queries; 3) infra check on MTU/packet loss and kube/VM eviction thresholds. We'll aim to have reproducer results by 2025-03-10.

[13:43] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[13:46] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the dashboard link and the reproducer runner.

End transcript.
